cards.front: Three layers that matter in system design
cards.back: Network (IP: where a packet goes), transport (TCP or UDP: how reliably) and application (HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket, DNS: what the bytes mean).
An L4 balancer sees only IPs and ports; an L7 balancer reads HTTP paths and headers.

cards.front: TCP vs UDP rule of thumb
cards.back: Use TCP unless a late packet is worthless. In a video call a frame 300 ms late is useless, so UDP lets the app skip it instead of waiting for a retransmit.
One lost segment stalls everything behind it on that connection, because TCP delivers in order.
Multiplexing: many requests interleaved on one TCP connection, with binary framing and header compression. One lost TCP packet still stalls every stream.
HTTP over QUIC on UDP. Streams are independent, the transport and TLS handshakes merge into one round trip, and connections survive a Wi-Fi to mobile switch.

cards.front: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC in one line
cards.back: REST for public APIs and easy HTTP caching, GraphQL when many screens need different fields, gRPC with protobuf for service-to-service calls.
gRPC's binary payload format, typically 3 to 10× smaller than JSON and faster to parse.
One long HTTP response streaming events from server to client, with built-in reconnect by last event ID. Good for scores, notifications and token streams.
An HTTP request upgraded to a full-duplex connection over TCP. Good when both sides send often, like chat, but gateways become stateful.
Verify the signature on every call, handle each event idempotently by its event ID, and reconcile anything still pending because a webhook can be lost.
Every 20 to 30 seconds, treating two missed heartbeats as a disconnect, because NATs and load balancers drop idle connections silently.

quiz.q: You deploy a WebSocket gateway and a million clients reconnect in the same second. What prevents this next time?
choices: Drain connections slowly and reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter
quiz.why: Slow draining plus jittered backoff spreads the reconnect load out.

quiz.q: A live-score page needs one-way updates to many browsers. Which is the simplest good fit?
quiz.why: SSE streams server-to-client events over HTTP with built-in reconnect.

quiz.q: A client timed out on POST /payments and retried, creating two payments. What was missing?
choices: An idempotency key deduped on the server
quiz.why: A timeout does not mean failure; idempotency keys make retries safe.

quiz.q: On a lossy mobile network, why can HTTP/3 beat HTTP/2?
choices: Loss on one QUIC stream does not block the others
quiz.why: HTTP/2 still suffers TCP head-of-line blocking; QUIC streams are independent.

quiz.q: Which API style is hardest to cache in a CDN?
choices: GraphQL, where everything is a POST to one URL
quiz.why: HTTP caches understand GET; GraphQL queries are POSTs to one endpoint.

quiz.q: Your app makes ten sequential calls to a server 150 ms away. What is the best fix?
choices: Batch them, for example a backend-for-frontend endpoint for the screen
quiz.why: Ten round trips at 150 ms is 1.5 s before any work; gather the screen's data in one call.

quiz.q: A payment processor lets you register a URL that it calls when a payment settles. Which pattern is this?
quiz.why: A webhook replaces polling between companies: the provider POSTs to your endpoint.
